entities.summary:
Alexander Freiherr von Spaen (d. 1692) was a preeminent Generalfeldmarschall of Brandenburg-Prussia, whose military career spanned the reigns of the Great Elector, Frederick William, and his son, Frederick I. Born into a noble family from the County of Mark, Spaen dedicated over three decades to the nascent Brandenburgian army, playing a pivotal role in its transformation from a modest territorial force into a respected European military power. His service was critical during a period of intense geopolitical upheaval in Central and Western Europe, marked by the expansionist policies of Louis XIV's France and the persistent threat from the Ottoman Empire.

Spaen's military prowess was demonstrated across numerous significant conflicts of the late 17th century. He distinguished himself during the Franco-Dutch War (1672–1678), notably commanding forces at the Battle of Fehrbellin in 1675, a decisive victory that cemented the Great Elector's reputation and Brandenburg's military capability. His leadership extended to the Great Turkish War, where he led Brandenburgian contingents in the relief of Vienna in 1683, a crucial moment in stemming the Ottoman advance into Central Europe. Later, during the Nine Years' War (1688–1697), Spaen commanded allied forces in the successful Siege of Bonn in 1689, further showcasing his strategic acumen and operational effectiveness.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Alexander von Spaen was a foundational figure in the development of the Brandenburg-Prussian military, whose leadership in key battles like Fehrbellin and the Siege of Bonn significantly contributed to Brandenburg's rise as a regional power and laid the groundwork for the future Prussian army.
